ogier-ghiselin-de-busbecq.name: Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq
ogier-ghiselin-de-busbecq.summary: A 16th-century Flemish diplomat and writer who served as ambassador to the Ottoman Empire and is credited with introducing tulips to Western Europe.

fernand-braudel.name: Fernand Braudel
fernand-braudel.summary: French historian (1902–1985) of the Annales School whose scholarship emphasized large-scale socioeconomic history, including works on the Mediterranean and on civilization and capitalism.

m-m-lig.name: Mămăligă
m-m-lig.summary: A dish of yellow maize flour traditional in Romania, Moldova, Hungary and Ukraine, similar to Italian polenta.

mount-athos.name: Mount Athos
mount-athos.summary: Mountain and self-governing monastic region in Greece, a major center of Eastern Orthodox monastic life since at least the 9th century.

ionian-islands.name: Ionian Islands
ionian-islands.summary: A group of islands in the Ionian Sea west of mainland Greece, long under Venetian rule before joining the Greek state in 1864.

cretan-school.name: Cretan School
cretan-school.summary: A school of icon painting, also called post-Byzantine art, that flourished in Venetian-ruled Crete and became the central force in Greek painting from the 15th to 17th centuries; its most famous member was El Greco.

james-athenian-stuart.name: James "Athenian" Stuart
james-athenian-stuart.summary: A British archaeologist, architect and artist (1713-1788) known for precise measured drawings of Ancient Greek buildings, pioneering Neoclassicism in Britain.

nicholas-revett.name: Nicholas Revett
nicholas-revett.summary: British architect (1720–1804) who documented the ruins of ancient Athens with James Stuart, helping revive interest in Greek architecture.

society-of-dilettanti.name: Society of Dilettanti
society-of-dilettanti.summary: A British society of noblemen and scholars, founded in 1734, that promoted the study of ancient Greek and Roman art and funded new work in that style.

el-greco.name: El Greco
el-greco.summary: A Greek-born painter, sculptor and architect (1541–1614) of the Spanish Renaissance, trained in Crete and Venice, who settled in Toledo, Spain, and produced his best-known works there.

great-turkish-war.name: Great Turkish War
great-turkish-war.summary: A 1683 to 1699 war in which the Holy League of European powers decisively defeated the Ottoman Empire, which lost substantial territory in Hungary and the Balkans for the first time.

pausanias-geographer.name: Pausanias (geographer)
pausanias-geographer.summary: A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer, c. 110 to 180, whose Description of Greece is a key source linking classical literature to archaeological sites.

julien-david-le-roy.name: Julien-David Le Roy
julien-david-le-roy.summary: 18th-century French architect and archaeologist who beat British rivals Stuart and Revett by four years in publishing the first professional survey of the Acropolis of Athens' ruins since an early 1682 study by Antoine Desgodetz.

republic-of-ragusa.name: Republic of Ragusa
republic-of-ragusa.summary: An aristocratic maritime republic centered on Dubrovnik, known as Ragusa in Italian and Latin, that existed from 1358 until conquered by Napoleon's forces in 1806-08.

orlov-revolt.name: Orlov Revolt
orlov-revolt.summary: A Greek uprising in the Peloponnese and Crete that broke out in 1770, backed by Russia during a war with the Ottomans, and suppressed by June 1771.

maniots.name: Maniots
maniots.summary: The traditional native Greek inhabitants of the Mani Peninsula in the southern Peloponnese, historically known as fierce, independent warriors who claim descent from the ancient Spartans.

peter-the-great.name: Peter the Great
peter-the-great.summary: Tsar of Russia from 1682 and its first emperor from 1721 until his death in 1725, who westernized Russia, built its navy, and founded St Petersburg.

russo-turkish-war-1710-1713.name: Pruth River Campaign
russo-turkish-war-1710-1713.summary: A brief 1711 conflict in which Tsar Peter I's army, after entering Ottoman-vassal Moldavia, was surrounded by Ottoman forces near the Pruth River and forced to abandon the fortress of Azov.

morea.name: Morea
morea.summary: The medieval and early modern name for the Peloponnese peninsula in southern Greece, used successively by the Byzantines, Ottomans and Venetians.

catherine-the-great.name: Catherine the Great
catherine-the-great.summary: Empress of Russia from 1762 to 1796, who seized power from her husband Peter III and oversaw an era of territorial expansion and Enlightenment reform.

lambros-katsonis.name: Lambros Katsonis
lambros-katsonis.summary: A Greek naval commander (1752-1805) who sailed under the Russian flag as a colonel, becoming a knight of the Russian Empire.

klepht.name: Klephts
klepht.summary: Highwaymen-turned-insurgents in Ottoman-ruled Greece, descended from Greeks who fled to the mountains in the 15th century; they fought Ottoman rule and remained active as brigands into the 19th century.

armatoles.name: Armatoles
armatoles.summary: Irregular militia commissioned by the Ottomans to enforce order in Greek regions, often recruited from former or rival bandits (klephts), holding semi-independent status.

erotokritos.name: Erotokritos
erotokritos.summary: A 10,000-line verse romance in the Cretan Greek dialect, written in the early 17th century by Vikentios Kornaros, considered a masterpiece of Cretan literature.

vitsentzos-kornaros.name: Vitsentzos Kornaros
vitsentzos-kornaros.summary: Cretan poet of Venetian origin (1553–1613/1614) who wrote the romantic epic Erotokritos in vernacular Cretan Greek, considered the greatest of the Cretan poets.

georgios-chortatzis.name: Georgios Chortatzis
georgios-chortatzis.summary: Greek dramatist (c. 1545-1610) writing in Cretan verse, best known for the tragedy Erofili, set in Egypt.

erofili.name: Erofili
erofili.summary: The most famous tragedy of Cretan literature, written around 1600 by Georgios Chortatzis and first published in Venice in 1637.

rigas-feraios.name: Rigas Feraios
rigas-feraios.summary: Greek writer, political thinker and revolutionary (1757–1798) active in the Modern Greek Enlightenment, remembered today as a national hero and pioneer of the Greek War of Independence.

dionysios-solomos.name: Dionysios Solomos
dionysios-solomos.summary: Greek poet (1798–1857) from Zakynthos considered Greece's national poet, best known for writing the Hymn to Liberty, which became the Greek national anthem in 1865.

hymn-to-liberty.name: Hymn to Liberty
hymn-to-liberty.summary: A Greek poem written in 1823 whose first two stanzas became the national anthem of Greece in 1864 and of Cyprus in 1966.

demotic-greek.name: Demotic Greek
demotic-greek.summary: The vernacular spoken form of Greek used by most Greeks in the 19th and 20th centuries, contrasted with formal Katharevousa, and made Greece's official language in 1976.

thyestes.name: Thyestes
thyestes.summary: A king of Olympia in Greek mythology who, with his brother Atreus, was exiled for murdering their half-brother, and whose story inspired Seneca's revenge tragedy in 62 CE.

adamantios-korais.name: Adamantios Korais
adamantios-korais.summary: Greek scholar (1748–1833) credited with laying the foundations of modern Greek literature and a major figure of the Greek Enlightenment, whose work helped pave the way for the Greek War of Independence.

giannitsa.name: Giannitsa
giannitsa.summary: A city of about 32,000 people in Central Macedonia, Greece, in the fertile Giannitsa-Thessaloniki plain, generally considered founded in the Byzantine period.

a-k-elebi.name: Aşık Çelebi
a-k-elebi.summary: An Ottoman biographer, poet and translator (1520–1572) born in Prizren, best known for his 1568 biographical work on poets, Senses of Poets.

prizren.name: Prizren
prizren.summary: The second most populous city in Kosovo and its constitutionally designated historical capital, it served as capital of the Serbian Empire under Stefan Dušan before falling to the Ottomans in 1455.

roger-joseph-boscovich.name: Roger Joseph Boscovich
roger-joseph-boscovich.summary: Physicist, astronomer and Jesuit priest (1711–1787) from Ragusa who produced an early precursor of atomic theory and discovered in 1753 that the Moon has no atmosphere.

eugenios-voulgaris.name: Eugenios Voulgaris
eugenios-voulgaris.summary: A Greek Orthodox cleric, author, educator and philosopher (1716–1806) who wrote across nearly every discipline, served as bishop of Cherson, and was a leading figure of the Modern Greek Enlightenment.

modern-greek-enlightenment.name: Modern Greek Enlightenment
modern-greek-enlightenment.summary: The Greek expression of the Age of Enlightenment, an intellectual movement among Greeks then scattered across the Ottoman Empire, the Ionian Islands, Venice and Italy, which served as its educational center.

athanasios-psalidas.name: Athanasios Psalidas
athanasios-psalidas.summary: Greek author and scholar (1767 to 1829), one of the most renowned figures of the modern Greek Enlightenment.

kaplaneios-school.name: Kaplaneios School
kaplaneios-school.summary: A Greek school in Ioannina, operating 1797 to 1820/21, originally named the Maroutsaia School, that became the city's leading intellectual centre under Athanasios Psalidas.

athonite-academy.name: Athonite Academy
athonite-academy.summary: Greek Orthodox school founded in 1749 at Mount Athos that taught ancient philosophy alongside modern science, leading the local monastic community's role in the Greek Enlightenment.

vatopedi.name: Vatopedi
vatopedi.summary: An Eastern Orthodox monastery on Mount Athos, Greece, expanded several times especially during the Byzantine period and the 18th and 19th centuries, home to more than 120 monks today.

methodios-anthrakites.name: Methodios Anthrakites
methodios-anthrakites.summary: A Greek Orthodox cleric, mathematician and philosopher (1660–1736) who directed schools in Ioannina, promoted modern philosophical thought in Greek education, and was persecuted for it in the so-called Methodios Affair.

least-absolute-deviations.name: Least absolute deviations
least-absolute-deviations.summary: A statistical method that fits a model by minimizing the sum of absolute errors rather than squared errors, introduced by Roger Joseph Boscovich in 1757.

suleiman-the-magnificent.name: Suleiman the Magnificent
suleiman-the-magnificent.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign brought the empire's greatest economic, military and political power and reformed its legal system.

battle-of-moh-cs.name: Battle of Mohács
battle-of-moh-cs.summary: A 29 August 1526 battle in which the Ottomans under Suleiman the Magnificent decisively defeated Hungary's King Louis II, ending the Jagiellonian dynasty there and leading to Hungary's partition.

wallachia.name: Wallachia
wallachia.summary: A historical Romanian principality south of the Carpathians that formed around the 13th century, became an Ottoman tributary in 1417, and united with Moldavia in 1859 to help found modern Romania.

moldavia.name: Moldavia
moldavia.summary: A historical principality in Eastern Europe under Ottoman overlordship from the 14th century to 1859, when it united with Wallachia to form the basis of modern Romania.

greek-project.name: Greek Project
greek-project.summary: A plan proposed by Catherine the Great in the early 1780s to partition the Ottoman Empire between Russia and the Habsburgs and restore a Byzantine Empire centered on Constantinople.

serbian-revolution.name: Serbian Revolution
serbian-revolution.summary: A national uprising and constitutional transformation in Serbia between 1804 and 1835 that turned an Ottoman province into a constitutional monarchy, sparked by the 1804 killing of Serbian nobles.

manuel-palaiologos.name: Manuel Palaiologos
manuel-palaiologos.summary: Youngest son of Thomas Palaiologos and nephew of the last Byzantine emperor Constantine XI; raised in exile in Italy, he returned to Ottoman Constantinople in 1476 and lived out his life there.

thomas-palaiologos.name: Thomas Palaiologos
thomas-palaiologos.summary: Brother of the last Byzantine emperor, he ruled as Despot of the Morea from 1428 until its fall to the Ottomans in 1460.

palaiologos.name: Palaiologos
palaiologos.summary: A Byzantine Greek noble family that produced the empire's last and longest-ruling dynasty, holding the throne from 1259 until Constantinople fell in 1453.

house-of-gonzaga.name: Gonzaga family
house-of-gonzaga.summary: An Italian princely family that ruled Mantua in northern Italy from 1328 to 1708, also holding Monferrato and Nevers, and producing two Holy Roman empresses.

palaeologus-montferrat.name: Palaeologus-Montferrat family
palaeologus-montferrat.summary: An Italian noble family descended from a Byzantine prince who inherited the March of Montferrat in 1306, giving it a claim to the Byzantine imperial legacy.

vincenzo-ii-gonzaga.name: Vincenzo II Gonzaga
vincenzo-ii-gonzaga.summary: Duke of Mantua and Duke of Montferrat from 1626 until his death in 1627; he briefly held a cardinalate before marrying and died without children.

charles-i-gonzaga.name: Charles I Gonzaga
charles-i-gonzaga.summary: Duke of Mantua and Montferrat from 1627 to 1637, also known as Charles III as Duke of Nevers and Rethel and Prince of Arche and Charleville.

theophilos-corydalleus.name: Theophilos Corydalleus
theophilos-corydalleus.summary: A Greek Neo-Aristotelian philosopher (1574–1646) and Orthodox cleric whose teachings, known as Korydalism, shaped Greek education for two centuries.

iosipos-moisiodax.name: Iosipos Moisiodax
iosipos-moisiodax.summary: Greek and later Wallachian philosopher and Orthodox deacon (1725–1800), a leading figure of the modern Greek Enlightenment who led academies in Iași and Bucharest.

ren-descartes.name: René Descartes
ren-descartes.summary: A French philosopher, mathematician and scientist (1596–1650) known for "I think, therefore I am" and for founding analytic geometry.

galileo-galilei.name: Galileo Galilei
galileo-galilei.summary: An Italian astronomer, physicist, and polymath (1564–1642) called the father of observational astronomy and modern science, whose telescope discoveries and support for heliocentrism led to conflict with the Catholic Church.

john-locke.name: John Locke
john-locke.summary: English Enlightenment philosopher and physician, called the father of liberalism, whose writings on toleration and government by consent of the governed influenced the American Declaration of Independence.

isaac-newton.name: Isaac Newton
isaac-newton.summary: English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727) whose 1687 Principia established the laws of motion and universal gravitation, founding classical mechanics.

cyril-lucaris.name: Cyril Lucaris
cyril-lucaris.summary: Greek Patriarch of Constantinople (1572–1638) who reportedly tried to reform the Eastern Orthodox Church along Calvinist lines, sparking lasting controversy within the Church.

ecumenical-patriarch-of-constantinople.name: Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople
ecumenical-patriarch-of-constantinople.summary: The archbishop of Constantinople and spiritual leader of Eastern Orthodox Christians worldwide, regarded as first among equals among Orthodox church heads.

synod-of-jerusalem-1672.name: Synod of Jerusalem
synod-of-jerusalem-1672.summary: An Eastern Orthodox council held in 1672 at Bethlehem that rejected Protestant doctrines and set out Orthodox teaching in response to the Reformation.

ia-i.name: Iași
ia-i.summary: Romania's third most populous city and former capital of Moldavia and, briefly, of Romania (1916–1918), long a leading centre of Romanian culture.

nectarius-of-jerusalem.name: Nectarius of Jerusalem
nectarius-of-jerusalem.summary: Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1661 to 1669, born Nikolaos Pelopidis in 1602.

dimitrios-katartzis.name: Dimitrios Katartzis
dimitrios-katartzis.summary: Phanariote Greek scholar, 1730 to 1807, who held administrative offices in Wallachia and championed the vernacular Greek language, arguing that pride in language reflected pride in a shared national identity.

nicholas-mavrocordatos.name: Nicholas Mavrocordatos
nicholas-mavrocordatos.summary: Greek member of the Mavrocordatos family who became Grand Dragoman to the Divan in 1697 and the first Phanariot ruling prince of the Danubian Principalities, serving twice each as Prince of Moldavia and Wallachia.

millet-ottoman-empire.name: Millet
millet-ottoman-empire.summary: In the Ottoman Empire, an autonomous legal community allowing non-Muslim religious groups to govern themselves under their own laws, later used from the 19th century for protected ethnic minority groups.

rum-millet.name: Rum Millet
rum-millet.summary: The Ottoman Empire's Eastern Orthodox Christian community, encompassing Greeks, Bulgarians, Albanians, Georgians, Serbs and others, which retained a degree of internal autonomy.

epirus.name: Epirus
epirus.summary: Rugged, mountainous region of southeastern Europe, now shared by Greece and Albania. It was home to the oracle of Dodona and became famous under Pyrrhus, who fought Rome, before joining the Roman Republic in 146 BC.

devshirme.name: Devshirme
devshirme.summary: Ottoman "child levy", first mentioned in written records in 1438. It produced a loyal faction of soldiers and officials, including many grand viziers, provincial governors and military commanders, who were easier for sultans to control.

phanariots.name: Phanariots
phanariots.summary: Prominent Greek families of Constantinople's Phanar quarter who held top Ottoman posts, such as rulers of Moldavia and Wallachia. They emerged as wealthy merchants in the late 1500s and dominated the Patriarchate's administration.

fener.name: Fener (Phanar)
fener.summary: Quarter midway up the Golden Horn in Istanbul, traditionally Greek in the Ottoman era. Its name comes from the Greek word for lantern, after a lantern-topped column that stood there in Byzantine times.

san-giorgio-dei-greci.name: San Giorgio dei Greci
san-giorgio-dei-greci.summary: Church in Venice built as the center of the city's Greek community and their Scuola dei Greci confraternity.

janissary.name: Janissaries
janissary.summary: Elite Ottoman infantry corps, among the first standing armies equipped mainly with firearms, recruited as boys from Christian families and converted to Islam; the corps was disbanded in 1826.

hagia-sophia.name: Hagia Sophia
hagia-sophia.summary: A monumental building in Istanbul completed in 537 CE, serving in turn as a Byzantine cathedral, a mosque, a museum, and again a mosque since 2020.

bektashism.name: Bektashism
bektashism.summary: A Sufi order of Islam that developed in 13th-century western Anatolia, named after the saint Haji Bektash Veli, and spread widely through the Ottoman Empire.

haji-bektash-veli.name: Haji Bektash Veli
haji-bektash-veli.summary: An Islamic scholar, mystic and philosopher from Khorasan who lived and taught in Anatolia around 1209 to 1271, revered by Alevis and seen as the eponym of the Bektashi Sufi order.

constantine-mavrocordatos.name: Constantine Mavrocordatos
constantine-mavrocordatos.summary: Greek noble (1711 to 1769) who served as prince of Wallachia and of Moldavia at several intervals between 1730 and 1769. His reforms included fairer taxation and more humane treatment of slaves.

alexander-ypsilantis-1725-1805.name: Alexander Ypsilantis
alexander-ypsilantis-1725-1805.summary: Greek prince of Wallachia from 1774 to 1782 and again from 1796 to 1797, and of Moldavia from 1786 to 1788. He belonged to the prominent Phanariote Ypsilantis family.

danubian-principalities.name: Danubian Principalities
danubian-principalities.summary: Term for the Ottoman vassal principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia from 1774 to 1858, a battleground between the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires. They were unified in 1859.

charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.name: Charles V
charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (1500–1558) whose Habsburg realms in Europe and the Americas were together called 'the empire on which the sun never sets'.

martin-crusius.name: Martin Crusius
martin-crusius.summary: German classicist and historian (1524–1607) and professor at the University of Tübingen from 1559. A follower of Philip Melanchthon, he also wrote a commentary on the Iliad.
